# Air and Combustion

## Core ideas and reasoning

Dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% other gases by volume, with variable water vapour in ordinary air. Combustion is reaction with oxygen that releases energy; other forms of oxidation may occur slowly without a flame. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in sufficient oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water. Limited oxygen can form toxic carbon monoxide and soot. Burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide; oxide behaviour depends on the element, with many metal oxides basic and many nonmetal oxides acidic. Test oxygen using a glowing splint, which relights under suitable conditions. Test carbon dioxide using limewater, which becomes milky due to calcium carbonate. Excess carbon dioxide may later dissolve the precipitate. Rusting of iron needs both oxygen and water; coatings exclude them, galvanising also offers sacrificial protection. A change in gas volume in an experiment must account for cooling, pressure and gases absorbed, not simply attribute all loss to oxygen.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Name the two most abundant gases in dry air with approximate percentages.

Nitrogen about 78% and oxygen about 21% by volume.

### Example 2

Write the balanced equation for complete combustion of methane.

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O. Count C:1, H:4 and O:4 on each side.

### Example 3

State the conditions necessary for rusting iron and one prevention method.

Oxygen and water are both needed. Painting prevents contact with them when the coating is intact.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
